source_text: οἱ πολλοὶ δὲ τῇ τῶν χειμώνων καταστάσει ὁμοίαν ἔχουσι τὴν διάθεσιν ἀνέδραστόν τε καὶ ἀλόγιστον. Πολλὰ ἀπιστία δέδρακεν ἀγαθὰ καὶ πίστις κακά. ὅ τε Ἐπίχαρμος μέμνασο ἀπιστεῖν φησίν· ἄρθρα ταῦτα τῶν φρενῶν. αὐτίκα τὸ μὲν ἀπιστεῖν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ θάνατον φέρει ὡς τὸ πιστεύειν ζωήν, ἔμπαλιν δὲ τὸ πιστεύειν τῷ ψεύδει, ἀπιστεῖν δὲ τῇ ἀληθείᾳ εἰς ἀπώλειαν ὑποσύρει. ὁ αὐτὸς λόγος ἐπί τε ἐγκρατείας καὶ ἀκρασίας. ἐγκρατεύεσθαι μὲν γὰρ ἀγαθοεργίας κακίας ἔργον, ἀπέχεσθαι δὲ ἀδικίας σωτηρίας ἀρχή. ᾗ μοι δοκεῖ τὸ σάββατον δἰ ἀποχῆς κακῶν ἐγκράτειαν αἰνίσσεσθαι καὶ τί ποτ’ ἐστὶν ᾧ διαφέρει θηρίων ἄνθρωπος. τούτου τε αὖ οἱ τοῦ θεοῦ ἄγγελοι σοφώτεροι· ἠλάττωσας αὐτόν, φησί, βραχύ τι παρ’ ἀγγέλους· οὐ γὰρ ἐπὶ τοῦ κυρίου ἐκδέχονται τὴν γραφήν *καίτοι κἀκεῖνος σάρκα ἔφερεν), ἐπὶ δὲ τοῦ τελείου καὶ γνωστικοῦ τῷ χρόνῳ καὶ τῷ ἐνδύματι ἐλαττουμένου παρὰ τοὺς ἀγγέλους. οὐκοῦν ἄλλο τι σοφίαν παρὰ τὴν ἐπιστήμην λέγω, ἐπεὶ μὴ διαφέρει ζωή· κοινὸν γὰρ τῇ φύσει τῇ θνητῇ, τουτέστι τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ, πρὸς τὸ ἀθανασίας κατηξιωμένον τὸ ζῆν, ἕξιν θεωρίας τε καὶ ἐγκρατείας θατέρου διαφέροντος. ᾗ μοι δοκεῖ καὶ Πυθαγόρας σοφὸν μὲν εἶναι τὸν θεὸν λέγειν μόνον (ἐπεὶ καὶ ὁ ἀπόστολος ἐν τῇ πρὸς Ῥωμαίους ἐπιστολῇ γράφει· εἰς ὑπακοὴν πίστεως εἰς πάντα τὰ ἔθνη γνωρισθέντος, μόνῳ σοφῷ θεῷ διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ), ἑαυτὸν δὲ διὰ φιλίαν τὴν πρὸς τὸν θεὸν φιλόσοφον. διελέγετο γοῦν Μωυσεῖ, φησίν, ὁ θεὸς ὡς φίλος φίλῳ. τὸ μὲν οὖν ἀληθὲς τῷ θεῷ σαφές. αὐτίκα τὴν ἀλήθειαν γεννᾷ, ὁ γνωστικὸς δὲ ἀληθείας ἐρᾷ. ἴσθι, φησί, πρὸς τὸν μύρμηκα, ὦ ὀκνηρέ, καὶ μελίττης γενοῦ μαθητής, ὁ Σολομὼν λέγει· εἰ γὰρ ἑκάστου τῆς οἰκείας φύσεως ἔργον ἓν καὶ βοὸς ὁμοίως καὶ ἵππου καὶ κυνός, τί ἂν φήσαιμεν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τὸ ἔργον τὸ οἰκεῖον; ἔοικεν δ’ οἶμαι, κενταύρῳ, Θετταλικῷ πλάσματι, ἐκ λογικοῦ καὶ ἀλόγου συγκείμενος, ψυχῆς καὶ σώματος, ἀλλὰ τὸ μὲν σῶμα γῆν τε ἐργάζεται καὶ σπεύδει εἰς γῆν, τέταται δὲ ἡ ψυχὴ πρὸς τὸν θεόν, ἥ γε διὰ φιλοσοφίας τῆς ἀληθοῦς παιδευομένη, πρός τε τοὺς ἄνω σπεύδει συγγενεῖς, ἀποστραφεῖσα τῶν τοῦ σώματος ἐπιθυμιῶν πρός τε ταύταις πόνου τε καὶ φόβου· καίτοι πρὸς ἀγαθοῦ καὶ τὴν ὑπομονὴν καὶ τὸν φόβον ἐδείξαμεν. εἰ γὰρ διὰ νόμου ἐπίγνωσις ἁμαρτίας, ὡς οἱ κατατρέχοντες τοῦ νόμου φασί, καὶ ›ἄχρι νόμου ἁμαρτία ἦν ἐν κόσμῳ,‹ ἀλλὰ ›χωρὶς νόμου ἁμαρτία νεκρὰ‹ ἀντᾴδομεν αὐτοῖς. ὅταν γὰρ ἀφέλῃς τὸ αἴτιον τοῦ φόβου, τὴν ἁμαρτίαν, ἀφεῖλες τὸν φόβον, πολὺ δὲ ἔτι μᾶλλον τὴν κόλασιν, ὅταν ἀπῇ τὸ πεφυκὸς ἐπιθυμεῖν· δικαίῳ γὰρ οὐ κεῖται νόμος, ἡ γραφή φησιν. καλῶς οὖν Ἡράκλειτος δίκης ὄνομα φησὶν οὐκ ἂν ᾔδεσαν, εἰ ταῦτα μὴ ἦν, Σωκράτης δὲ νόμον ἕνεκα ἀγαθῶν οὐκ ἂν γενέσθαι. ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ τοῦτο ἔγνωσαν οἱ κατήγοροι, ὡς ὁ ἀπόστολός φησιν ὅτι ὁ ἀγαπῶν τὸν πλησίον κακὸν οὐκ ἐργάζεται· τὸ γὰρ οὐ φονεύσεις, οὐ μοιχεύσεις, οὐ κλέψεις, καὶ εἴ τις ἑτέρα ἐντολή, ἐν τούτῳ μόνῳ ἀνακεφαλαιοῦται τῷ λόγῳ, τῷ· ›ἀγαπήσεις τὸν πλησίον σου ὡς σεαυτόν.‹ ταύτῃ που ἀγαπήσεις κύριον τὸν θεόν σου φησὶν ἐξ ὅλης καρδίας σου, καὶ ἀγαπήσεις τὸν πλησίον σου ὡς σεαυτόν. εἰ δὴ ὁ τὸν πλησίον ἀγαπῶν κακὸν οὐκ ἐργάζεται καὶ πᾶσα ἐντολὴ ἐν τούτῳ ἀνακεφαλαιοῦται, τῷ ἀγαπᾶν τὸν πλησίον, αἱ τὸν φόβον ἐπαρτῶσαι ἐντολαὶ ἀγάπην, οὐ μῖσος κατασκευάζουσιν. οὔκουν πάθος ὁ φόβος οὗ γεννητικὸς ὁ νόμος. ὥστε ὁ νόμος ἅγιος καὶ τῷ ὄντι πνευματικός ἐστι κατὰ τὸν ἀπόστολον. δεῖ δή, ὡς ἔοικε, τήν γε τοῦ σώματος φύσιν καὶ τὴν τῆς ψυχῆς οὐσίαν πολυπραγμονήσαντας τὸ ἑκατέρου τέλος καταλαβέσθαι καὶ μὴ τὸν θάνατον ἡγεῖσθαι κακόν· ὅτε γὰρ δοῦλοι ἦτε τῆς ἁμαρτίας, φησὶν ὁ ἀπόστολος, ἐλεύθεροι ἦτε τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ. τίνα οὖν καρπὸν εἴχετε τότε; ἐφ’ οἷς νῦν ἐπαισχύνεσθε· τὸ γὰρ τέλος ἐκείνων θάνατος. νῦν δὲ ἐλευθερωθέντες ἀπὸ τῆς ἁμαρτίας, δουλωθέντες δὲ τῷ θεῷ, ἔχετε τὸν καρπὸν ὑμῶν εἰς ἁγιασμόν, τὸ δὲ τέλος ζωὴν αἰώνιον. τὰ γὰρ ὀψώνια τῆς ἁμαρτίας θάνατος, τὸ δὲ χάρισμα τοῦ θεοῦ ζωὴ αἰώνιος ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ τῷ κυρίῳ ἡμῶν. Κινδυνεύει τοίνυν δεδεῖχθαι θάνατος μὲν εἶναι ἡ ἐν σώματι κοινωνία τῆς ψυχῆς ἁμαρτητικῆς οὔσης, ζωὴ δὲ ὁ χωρισμὸς τῆς ἁμαρτίας. πολλοὶ δὲ οἱ ἐν ποσὶ χάρακες καὶ τάφροι τῆς ἐπιθυμίας τά τε ὀργῆς καὶ θυμοῦ βάραθρα, ἃ διαπηδᾶν ἀνάγκη καὶ πᾶσαν ἀποφεύγειν τὴν τῶν ἐπιβουλῶν ἀνασκευὴν τὸν μηκέτι δἰ ἐσόπτρου τὴν γνῶσιν τοῦ θεοῦ κατοψόμενον· ἥμισυ γάρ τ’ ἀρετῆς ἀποαίνυται εὐρύοπα Ζεὺς ἀνέρος, εὖτ’ ἄν μιν κατὰ δούλιον ἦμαρ ἕλῃσι. δούλους δὲ τοὺς ὑπὸ ἁμαρτίαν καὶ ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις πεπραμένους, τοὺς φιληδόνους καὶ φιλοσωμάτους οἶδεν ἡ γραφή, καὶ θηρία μᾶλλον ἢ ἀνθρώπους, τοὺς παρομοιωθέντας τοῖς κτήνεσι, θηλυμανεῖς ἵππους ἐπὶ τὰς τῶν πλησίον χρεμετίζοντας· ὄνος ὑβριστὴς ὁ ἀκόλαστος, λύκος ἄγριος ὁ πλεονεκτικὸς καὶ ὄφις ὁ ἀπατεών. ὁ τοίνυν ἀπὸ τοῦ σώματος τῆς ψυχῆς χωρισμὸς ὁ παρ’ ὅλον τὸν βίον μελετώμενος τῷ φιλοσόφῳ προθυμίαν κατασκευάζει γνωστικὴν εὐκόλως δύνασθαι φέρειν τὸν τῆς φύσεως θάνατον, διάλυσιν ὄντα τῶν πρὸς τὸ σῶμα τῆς ψυχῆς δεσμῶν· ἐμοὶ γὰρ κόσμος ἐσταύρωται κἀγὼ τῷ κόσμῳ λέγει, βιῶ δὲ ἤδη ἐν σαρκὶ ὢν ὡς ἐν οὐρανῷ πολιτευόμενος.
thought_title: The Nature of Humanity and Virtue
pass_a_gloss: The many have a disposition similar to the stability of winters, uncontrolled and irrational. Unbelief has done many good things and faith has done bad things. Also, Epicharmus says to remember to disbelieve, for these are the joints of the mind. Immediately, disbelieving the truth brings death, just as believing brings life. On the other hand, believing a lie and disbelieving the truth leads to destruction. The same argument applies to self-control and lack of self-control. For self-control is a work of good deeds, and abstaining from injustice is the beginning of salvation. It seems to me that the Sabbath, through abstaining from evil, praises self-control and asks what distinguishes humans from beasts. The angels of God are wiser than humans, for it is said, 'You have made him a little lower than the angels.' They do not expect the scripture concerning the Lord, even though He wore flesh, but concerning the perfect and knowledgeable one, who is lessened in time and clothing compared to the angels. I say that wisdom is something other than knowledge, since life does not differ. For mortal nature, that is, humanity, has been deemed worthy of immortality, living with the habit of contemplation and self-control, which differs from the other. It seems to me that even Pythagoras says that only God is wise, and that he himself is a philosopher through friendship with God. For it is said that God spoke to Moses as a friend to a friend. The truth is clear to God. Immediately, truth generates, and the knowledgeable one desires truth. Solomon says, 'Be aware, you lazy one, and become a student of the ant and the bee.' For if each one's work is one and the same, whether of an ox or a horse or a dog, what would we say is the work of humanity? It seems to me that humanity is like a centaur, a Thessalian creation, composed of rational and irrational parts, soul and body. However, the body works the earth and hastens towards the earth, while the soul is stretched towards God, and through true philosophy, it is educated, hastening towards the things above, having turned away from the desires of the body, and towards the pains and fears. Although we have shown that endurance and fear are good. For if knowledge of sin is through the law, as those who pursue the law say, and 'sin was in the world until the law,' but 'sin is dead without the law,' we respond to them. When you remove the cause of fear, sin, you have removed fear, and much more so punishment, when you remove the natural desire. For the law is not laid down for the righteous, the scripture says. Heraclitus says that the name of justice would not have been known if these things did not exist. Socrates says that the law would not have been created for the sake of good things. But the accusers did not know this, as the apostle says, that the one who loves their neighbor does not do evil. For the commandments 'do not kill, do not commit adultery, do not steal,' and if there is any other commandment, are all summed up in the word 'love your neighbor as yourself.' This is how you will love the Lord your God with all your heart and love your neighbor as yourself. If the one who loves their neighbor does not do evil, and every commandment is summed up in loving the neighbor, the commandments that inspire fear establish love, not hatred. Fear is not a passion, of which the law is the generator. Therefore, the law is holy and spiritual, according to the apostle. It is necessary, as it seems, to understand the nature of the body and the substance of the soul, and to grasp the end of each, and not to consider death an evil. For when you were slaves of sin, the apostle says, you were free from righteousness. What fruit did you have then? The things you are now ashamed of, for the end of those things is death. But now, having been freed from sin and enslaved to God, you have your fruit in sanctification, and the end is eternal life. For the wages of sin are death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. Therefore, it is clear that death is the communion of the soul with the body when it is sinful, and life is the separation from sin. Many people have trenches and ditches of desire, and pits of anger and passion, which it is necessary to jump over and avoid all the contrivance of plots, no longer looking at the knowledge of God through a mirror. For a man who is seized by a servile day loses half of virtue, as Zeus, who is far-seeing, takes it away. The scripture knows that those who are slaves to sin and have been sold to sins are lovers of pleasure and lovers of the body, and are more like beasts than humans, having been compared to animals, like uncontrolled horses rushing towards the things of their neighbors. The uncontrolled one is like a stubborn donkey, the greedy one is like a wild wolf, and the deceiver is like a snake. The separation of the soul from the body, which is practiced throughout life by the philosopher, creates a willingness to easily bear the death of nature, which is the dissolution of the bonds of the soul to the body. For the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world, and I live, being in the flesh, as if I were living in heaven, conducting my life as a citizen of heaven.

choices.why: The Greek word ἐγκρατεύεσθαι means to have control over one's desires and actions.
The Greek word ἀκρασία refers to the lack of control over one's desires and actions.
The Greek word ἀποχή means to abstain or refrain from something.
The Greek word ἐγκράτεια refers to the virtue of self-control.
The Greek word ἄγγελος means messenger or angel.

pass_b_english: Many people have a disposition like the stubbornness of winter, uncontrolled and irrational. Unbelief has accomplished many good things, and faith has accomplished bad ones. Remember Epicharmus's saying: 'Disbelieve, for these are the joints of the mind.' Disbelieving the truth brings death just as believing brings life; conversely, believing a lie and disbelieving the truth drags one down to destruction. The same reasoning applies to self-control and self-indulgence. Self-control produces good works, and abstaining from injustice is the beginning of salvation. It seems to me that the Sabbath, through abstinence from evil, signifies self-control and poses the question of what distinguishes human beings from beasts. In this respect the angels of God are wiser; Scripture says, 'You have made him a little lower than the angels' (Psalm 8:5). They do not await the Scripture's fulfillment in the Lord, even though He bore flesh, but in the perfect Gnostic who in time and clothing is made lower than the angels. I therefore affirm that wisdom is something other than mere knowledge, since life itself does not differ; mortal nature — that is, humanity — shares the common lot, yet has been deemed worthy of immortality by living with the habit of contemplation and self-control, which sets it apart. It seems to me that Pythagoras, too, says that God alone is wise (since the apostle writes in Romans of the mystery made known to all nations for the obedience of faith, 'to the only wise God through Jesus Christ,' Romans 16:26), while he calls himself a philosopher through friendship toward God. 'God spoke to Moses as a friend speaks to a friend' (Exodus 33:11). The truth is clear to God; truth begets, and the Gnostic loves truth. Solomon says, 'Go to the ant, you sluggard; consider its ways and be wise' (Proverbs 6:6), and become a disciple of the bee. If each creature has its single proper work — ox, horse, and dog alike — what shall we say is humanity's proper work? Humanity appears to me to resemble a centaur, a Thessalian composite of rational and irrational parts, soul and body. The body works the earth and hastens back to earth, but the soul stretches toward God; educated by true philosophy, it hastens toward its kindred above, turning away from the body's desires and toward the pains and fears that accompany them — though we have shown that endurance and fear can serve the good. If knowledge of sin comes through the law, as those who run after the law say, and 'sin was in the world until the law' (Romans 5:13), yet 'sin is dead apart from the law' (Romans 7:8), we answer them: when you remove the cause of fear — sin — you remove fear, and far more so punishment, when the natural desire is gone. 'The law is not laid down for the just,' Scripture says (1 Timothy 1:9). Heraclitus rightly says the name of justice would never have been known if these things did not exist; Socrates says law would not have been enacted for the sake of good things. Yet the accusers did not grasp this, as the apostle declares: 'The one who loves his neighbor does no evil' (Romans 13:10). For the commandments — 'You shall not murder, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal,' and any other commandment — are summed up in this word: 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself' (Galatians 5:14; Leviticus 19:18; Matthew 22:39). This is how you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and your neighbor as yourself (Matthew 22:37-40). If the one who loves his neighbor works no evil, and every commandment is summed up in loving the neighbor, then the commandments that implant fear produce love, not hatred. Fear is not a passion of which the law is the generator. Therefore the law is holy, and truly spiritual, according to the apostle (Romans 7:12, 14). It is necessary, as it seems, to investigate the body's nature and the soul's substance, to grasp the end of each, and not to regard death as an evil. 'When you were slaves of sin, you were free in regard to righteousness,' the apostle says (Romans 6:20). What fruit did you have then? Things you are now ashamed of, for the end of those things is death. But now, having been freed from sin and enslaved to God, you have your fruit for sanctification, and the end is eternal life (Romans 6:22). For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord (Romans 6:23). It follows that death is the soul's communion with the body while the soul is sinful, and life is separation from sin. Many have trenches and ditches of desire, and pits of anger and rage, which one must leap over and avoid every contrivance of plots, no longer beholding the knowledge of God through a mirror. 'Half of a man's virtue does wide-seeing Zeus take away when the day of slavery seizes him' (Homer, Odyssey 17.322-323). Scripture knows those who are under sin and sold into sins as lovers of pleasure and lovers of body, more beasts than men, likened to cattle — wanton horses neighing after their neighbors' possessions. The self-indulgent man is an insolent donkey, the covetous a wild wolf, the deceiver a snake. The soul's separation from the body, practiced throughout life by the philosopher, builds a readiness to bear natural death easily — the dissolution of the bonds between soul and body. 'The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world,' he says (Galatians 6:14), 'and I live, though in the flesh, as one who lives in heaven, conducting my life as a citizen of heaven' (Philippians 3:20).

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text, including the complex philosophical and theological arguments regarding the soul, the law, and the nature of sin. All scripture citations in Pass B are correctly identified and expanded from the Greek allusions (e.g., Psalm 8:5, Romans 16:26, Exodus 33:11, Proverbs 6:6, Romans 5:13, Romans 7:8, 1 Timothy 1:9, Romans 13:10, Galatians 5:14, Leviticus 19:18, Matthew 22:37-40, Romans 7:12, 14, Romans 6:20, Romans 6:22, Romans 6:23, Galatians 6:14, Philippians 3:20). The Homeric allusion (Odyssey 17.322-323) is correctly identified in Pass B. Pass A and B are consistent with the Greek source.
